characterList.description: A white male with reddish hair and glasses wearing a light grey t-shirt with two giraffes forming a heart with their necks
characterList.name: John Green

content_metadata.description: John Green discusses the concept of climate change, using probability curves to illustrate how global warming affects weather patterns.

qAndA.answer: He uses a black marker to draw the first probability curve, and then red and blue to draw two additional curves representing the probability in different scenarios.
qAndA.question: What color is the marker John Green uses to draw the probability curve?

qAndA.answer: He mentions the landfall of Hurricane Katrina in New Orleans.
qAndA.question: What is the event John Green mentions that occurred in 2005?

qAndA.answer: He states that due to the shifting probability curves, areas that were previously considered safe from flooding may become more prone to them, making it harder for homeowners to obtain insurance as the traditional risk assessments used by insurance companies will become obsolete.
qAndA.question: Why does John Green say that homes in safe areas might become difficult to insure?

qAndA.answer: John Green begins the video with a serious and focused demeanor, reflecting the weight of the topic of climate change. As he transitions into plugging his various projects, his mood shifts to become more lighthearted and playful, suggesting a sense of relief after addressing a complex and potentially daunting issue.
qAndA.question: How does John Green's mood shift from the beginning to the end of the video?

qAndA.answer: He is wearing a t-shirt that depicts two giraffes forming a heart with their necks.
qAndA.question: What animal is on the new t-shirt John Green is wearing?

characterInteraction.description: John Green directly addresses the camera, maintaining eye contact with the viewers.

scenes.contextualRelevance: John Green initiates a discussion about the effects of a warmer Earth on weather patterns.

narrativeProgression.description: John Green starts the video talking directly to the camera. He asks the viewers for four minutes of their time to have a conversation about climate change.
He assures the viewers that nobody is at fault for not fully grasping the intricacies of the subject he is about to discuss.

scenes.title: Introduction to Climate Change

characterInteraction.description: John Green continues talking directly to the camera

scenes.contextualRelevance: John Green uses the example of hurricane frequency to illustrate the concept of probability distributions.

narrativeProgression.description: John Green explains that the number of hurricanes hitting the US in a year is a random event and the only thing we can know is its probability.
He proceeds to draw a probability distribution curve of the number of major storms that hit the US in a given year over a period of 50 years.
John Green mentions the year 2005, the year Hurricane Katrina hit New Orleans
He finishes the drawing and shows the resulting bell curve to the viewers
He introduces the concept of probability distribution

scenes.title: Probability and Hurricanes

videoEditingDetails.description: Cut to John Green drawing on a notebook

characterInteraction.description: John Green continues talking directly to the camera

scenes.contextualRelevance: John Green illustrates how climate change alters the probability distribution of extreme weather events.

narrativeProgression.description: John Green continues his explanation stating that we should not focus on the specific events, but rather on the probability curve.
He then proceeds to illustrate how climate change does not mean that the previous occurrences are no longer possible, but that their probability changes.

scenes.thematicElements: Probability vs. Individual Events, Shifting Probabilities
scenes.title: Shifting Probabilities

videoEditingDetails.description: Cut back to John Green talking directly to the camera

scenes.contextualRelevance: John Green connects the shift in probability curves to the real-world consequence of increased flood risks.

narrativeProgression.description: John Green finishes drawing the probability curve of major storms in a warmer Earth and explains how this affects the 100-year floods that are used to decide if an area is safe from flooding.
John Green shifts the focus to a practical implication of the changing probability curve: flood risks and insurance.
He calls attention to the limitations of our current understanding and preparedness in the face of a changing climate, using the example of insurance companies.

scenes.thematicElements: Climate Change and Flood Risks, Insurance and Risk Assessment
scenes.title: Implications of Probability Shifts

videoEditingDetails.description: Cut to John Green drawing on a notebook

characterInteraction.description: John Green continues talking directly to the camera

scenes.contextualRelevance: John Green's concluding remarks emphasize the need for acceptance and preparation in the face of a changing climate.

narrativeProgression.description: John Green goes back to the main point: climate change is a problem that needs to be understood and prepared for.
John Green concludes the primary discussion on probability curves and their implications for a changing climate.
He reiterates the importance of understanding and preparing for the shifts in probability curves as a way of adapting to the consequences of climate change.

scenes.thematicElements: Climate Change Adaptation, Uncertainty and Preparedness
scenes.title: Concluding Remarks

videoEditingDetails.description: Cut to John Green talking directly to the camera

activities.description: Showing the shirt he is wearing
Showing and playing with a fidget toy

characterInteraction.description: John Green continues talking directly to the camera

scenes.contextualRelevance: Scene consists of plugs of projects that John Green is currently involved with.

scenes.title: John Green's Plugs

climax.description: John Green concludes the primary discussion on probability curves and their implications for a changing climate.

youtube_description:
Throughout this video I say "probability curve" when a statistician would say "probability distribution." I just want to say that I'm aware of this, and that it's a choice I intentionally made because I felt like it made it easier to understand. 

While I would very much like to get deep into probability functions, what they mean, and how they work, I don't know if that's necessary to understand the world with curves. And this isn't just about climate and weather, pretty much everything is better understood if it's understood in terms of probability functions. And I generally like to see the world not for the collapsed reality dot, but for the function underneath. It's why winning at gambling always feels empty to me, I know that the underlying function has my losing even if happened to get lucky. So, in a way, gambling is always losing, even if you win. 

I know I'm an armchair statistician, and that lots of people will be annoyed by the language in this video, but I hope you can forgive me!
